title: Simulation with Isaac Sim & Isaac Lab
blurb: Tests why robots train in simulation, the three properties every simulator trades off, Isaac Sim against Isaac Lab and the open-source alternatives, domain randomization and how to scope it, synthetic data, and what the payload experiment showed.

questions.prompt: Which problems with training on real hardware does simulation solve? Select all that apply.
options: It is unsafe while the policy is still bad
It gives physics that are too accurate
It is expensive, since robots break
It is slow, one trial at a time in real time
questions.explanation: Simulation runs many trials in parallel, faster than real time, with no physical risk. Its cost is the opposite of the fourth option: its physics are never exact.

questions.prompt: For a policy that only sees joint angles and velocities, which simulator property matters least?
options: Physics accuracy
Speed and parallelism
Contact dynamics
Rendering fidelity
questions.explanation: Photorealism matters for vision policies, not for one that never sees an image. Paying for ray tracing gives it nothing.

questions.prompt: What does Isaac Lab add on top of Isaac Sim?
options: Thousands of parallel RL environments
PhysX contact physics for rigid bodies
Ray-traced rendering of robot scenes
A licence to run Isaac Sim on CPUs
questions.explanation: Isaac Sim is the simulation and rendering platform with PhysX. Isaac Lab wraps it as learning environments and runs many in parallel.

questions.prompt: A learner has no GPU and no Isaac licence. What does the chapter suggest for learning the concepts?
options: MuJoCo or PyBullet
Training directly on a real robot
Isaac Lab in CPU mode
Gazebo with ray-traced rendering
questions.explanation: MuJoCo is free with fast contact physics, and PyBullet is light for prototyping. The book leans on Isaac because of production workflows, not because the others fall short for learning.

questions.prompt: In an Isaac Lab environment, which config holds the domain randomization triggers?
options: TerminationsCfg
RewardsCfg
SceneCfg
EventsCfg or RandomizationCfg
questions.explanation: Each concern is its own small config. Randomization can be swapped without touching rewards, terminations or the scene.

questions.prompt: Why does a policy trained in one fixed simulator often fail on real hardware?
options: Simulated robots always move faster than real ones.
The policy forgets its training once deployed.
Simulators can't model friction at all.
It exploits quirks that aren't real.
questions.explanation: Exploiting quirks lowers training loss, and the policy can't know they're not real. Randomization takes that option away.

questions.prompt: Why does randomizing simulator parameters push a policy toward features that hold in reality?
options: Overfitting to one setting now hurts on the others.
Randomization adds real-world data to training.
Randomized simulators are more physically accurate.
Randomized runs train for longer.
questions.explanation: To do well across the whole distribution, the policy must learn features robust to the variation, which tend to be closer to what also holds in reality.

questions.prompt: Which kinds of parameters does the chapter say can be randomized? Select all that apply.
options: Visuals, such as lighting, texture and camera intrinsics
The task's goal, changed every step without notice
Sensors, such as noise characteristics
Physics, such as friction, mass and motor strength
questions.explanation: The chapter lists physics, visual and sensor parameters. Randomizing the goal itself changes the task, not the simulator's fidelity.

questions.prompt: Where does Procedure 62.1 say to start?
options: With 2–4 parameters you trust least, centred on real estimates
With no randomization, adding it only after real failures
With every parameter you can think of, as wide as possible
With rendering parameters only, since vision dominates
questions.explanation: Start narrow, centre on the best real-world estimate, validate on hardware, then widen. Randomizing everything on day one is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: A policy can't learn anything at all in simulation after randomization is added. What does Procedure 62.1 suggest?
options: The range is too narrow. Widen it until learning starts.
The range is too wide. Narrow it, then widen slowly.
Switch to a more photorealistic simulator.
Remove the reward function and use demonstrations only.
questions.explanation: Too much variation too fast makes the problem unlearnable. Too little leaves the sim-to-real gap open.

questions.prompt: Why are synthetic labels from a simulator perfect?
options: Human labellers check every synthetic image.
It placed every object, so it knows the truth.
Synthetic data is only used for testing, not training.
Simulated images contain no noise of any kind.
questions.explanation: Boxes, masks and depth come free and exact. The cost is a visual gap to real images, which randomized rendering helps close.

questions.prompt: The randomized gains were designed for the geometric mean of 1 kg and 5 kg. What mass is that, in kg? Give two decimal places.
Mean overshoot was 10.0% for the fixed-config controller and 1.3% for the randomized one. About how many times lower is the randomized overshoot? Give one decimal place.
Where did the gap between the two controllers grow largest?
options: At the heaviest payload, 5 kg
At 2.24 kg, the randomized controller's design mass
At 1 kg, the fixed controller's own design point
It was the same at every mass tested
questions.explanation: At 5 kg, cost was 0.578 against 0.836 and overshoot 5.5% against 20.5%. At 1 kg the gap was small.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three properties that trade off in any robotics simulator (physics accuracy, rendering fidelity, speed/parallelism), and state which one matters "not at all" for a policy that only observes joint angles and velocities.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Physics accuracy, rendering fidelity, speed/parallelism. Rendering fidelity matters "not at all" for a policy that only observes joint angles and velocities, since it never receives any visual input for photorealism to affect.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain the difference between Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab in one or two sentences, and state which one you'd use for training a policy at scale.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Isaac Sim is the underlying simulation/rendering platform (physics engine, rendering); Isaac Lab is a robot-learning framework built on top of it that wraps scenes as standardised RL environments and runs thousands of parallel instances on one GPU. Isaac Lab is the one to use for training a policy at scale, since its parallelism is what makes large-scale RL training throughput practical.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's unloaded-mass comparison (fixed-config cost=0.46205 vs. domain-randomized cost=0.41036, both at the fixed-config's own exact design point), explain why this specific result is stronger evidence for domain randomization's value than the full-range comparison (0.6485 vs. 0.4937) alone would have been.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The full-range comparison (0.6485 vs. 0.4937) could in principle be explained by the domain-randomized controller simply being "better tuned overall" in a way that trades away performance at any single specific point. A skeptic could argue the fixed-config controller still wins where it was actually designed to win, and the average result is just an artifact of testing outside its intended range. The unloaded-mass comparison closes that exact loophole: it evaluates both controllers at the ONE condition the fixed-config controller was specifically designed for, with no "unfair range" objection available, and domain-randomized STILL wins (0.410 vs. 0.462), proving the earlier result isn't merely "fixed-config wins on its home turf but loses badly elsewhere," it's "domain-randomized wins essentially everywhere, including home turf."

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's heaviest-payload comparison (overshoot 20.54% fixed-config vs. 5.52% domain-randomized), explain in your own words what "overshoot" represents physically for a robot arm's controller, and why a 20.54% overshoot could be a safety concern in a real deployment.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Overshoot represents how far past the target position/setpoint the arm's actual position swings before settling. Physically, the arm moves further than commanded before correcting back, a direct consequence of a controller's gains being poorly matched to the actual mass being moved (heavier unexpected payload = more momentum than the controller "expects," causing it to overcorrect). A 20.54% overshoot in a real deployment is a safety concern because the arm's end effector could swing significantly past its intended position, risking collision with nearby objects, people, or the workpiece itself, especially in tight tolerances or shared human-robot workspaces where that extra swing wasn't accounted for.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague argues "if we tune our controller perfectly for the exact conditions we expect in deployment, that will always beat a domain-randomized controller tuned across a range we don't fully need." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own measured result shows the opposite: a controller tuned across a realistic payload-mass range beat the perfectly-matched single-condition controller even AT that exact matched condition (cost 0.410 vs. 0.462 at mass=1.0), not just elsewhere in the range. Tuning narrowly for one expected condition risks the controller learning to exploit that specific condition's quirks in a way that doesn't generalize even when the deployment conditions are close to, but not exactly, what was assumed, so a range-robust tuning approach is worth testing even when the target condition seems well known."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 62.1 warns against randomizing every parameter on day one. Using this chapter's Worked Example (which randomized a single parameter, payload mass), describe what evidence would justify adding a second randomized parameter (e.g. friction) to this specific controller-tuning task.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Evidence justifying adding friction as a second randomized parameter would be: real-hardware validation testing (Procedure 62.1 step 3) showing worse-than-simulated performance specifically traceable to friction mismatches (e.g. slippage or drag not predicted by the single-parameter-randomized simulation), or a documented, well-founded uncertainty about the actual friction coefficients of the real deployment surface/joints that wasn't captured by mass randomization alone. In either case, concrete evidence that mass randomization alone left a real, measurable sim-to-real gap traceable to friction specifically, rather than simply adding more parameters preemptively without evidence they matter for this task.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about MuJoCo's MJX (JAX-based) parallel simulation capability, mentioned in this chapter's Exposition. Explain in your own words how running physics simulation on a GPU via JAX differs from Isaac Lab's GPU-parallel approach, and what a learner without an Isaac licence gains by using it instead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: MuJoCo's MJX reimplements MuJoCo's physics in JAX, enabling the same kind of GPU-parallel simulation (many environment instances run simultaneously as batched array operations) that Isaac Lab provides, but built on JAX's functional, differentiable-programming ecosystem rather than Isaac Sim's Omniverse/USD/PhysX stack. This means MJX can run on a GPU without requiring an NVIDIA Isaac licence or the heavier Omniverse platform, and integrates naturally with JAX-based RL research code. A learner without an Isaac licence gains GPU-parallel simulation throughput (thousands of environments at once, the key advantage over single-instance CPU MuJoCo) using an entirely open-source stack, at the cost of MuJoCo's simpler, non-photorealistic rendering compared to Isaac Sim's ray-traced visuals.
